headlines.article_text: Sanofi to buy Insmed in pharma’s biggest deal in three years Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points U.S. drugmaker Insmed's shares rose on Tuesday after it was announced it would be acquired by Sanofi. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash for the respiratory disease specialist drugmaker. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023. In this article INSM SNY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023. The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash. It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff , when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023. Insmed shares closed up 14.1% at $170.15 on Tuesday, while Sanofi stock closed up 10.9% in Paris. 'Buys time' Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said. Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete. Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026 , as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026. While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity. Sanofi/Insmed shares over the past 12 months. "Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday. headlines.article_text: Anthropic stock sinks below $83 IPO price Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic stock sank on Tuesday, falling below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price. Shares of ANT have been dropping steadily since the stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq. Analysts are still bullish about the company, citing its potential to capture a large addressable market. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei inside the Nasdaq MarketSite ahead of the anticipated IPO of artificial intelligence company Anthropic in New York City on November 19, 2026. Charly Triballeau | Afp | Getty Images Shares of Anthropic closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price. The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout. Anthropic's initial public offering was oversubscribed, and roughly half of the institutional investors that placed orders for the stock were left empty-handed, as CNBC previously reported . But at least for now, as the market wavers, those firms don't appear to be racing to scoop up shares. Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday. Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target. "The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market." "While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme." Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock. They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company. "While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.
